findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2027-29 updated for announcement, 16/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review removes business rate growth benefit and New Homes Bonus ending create £3.861m annual deficit for 2027/28.
findings.detail: Government changes to local authority funding allocations have structurally reduced monies available to the council. Business rate growth has been rebased, removing a significant recurring funding benefit. New Homes Bonus has ended entirely with no continuing income. A one-off £1 million transitional protection grant was provided in 2026/27 but Government has confirmed this was one-off. The resulting deficit stands at £3.861 million for 2027/28.
findings.matters: These are structural, recurring losses of income, not temporary shortfalls; they show councils' vulnerability to government funding allocation changes; they explain why a historically prudent council with strong reserves now faces a material budget gap.
findings.figures: £3.861m annual deficit 2027/28; business rate rebasing; New Homes Bonus ended; £1m one-off 2026/27 not repeated
findings.quote: Changes made by Government in local authority funding allocations has significantly reduced monies available to EDDC in the time remaining before Local Government Reorganisation. business rate growth has been rebased with this significant funding benefit falling away. New Homes Bonus: no continuing income, this incentive grant has ended.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2027-29 updated for announcement, 16/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation likely delayed by at least one year, requiring council to set budget for additional 2028/29 year.
findings.detail: Secretary of State announced on 7 September 2026 a pause and review of the Local Government Reorganisation programme for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay. The council had expected to be absorbed into new unitary authorities for April 2028; the delay means it must now budget for 2028/29 under its own auspices. This reverses the assumption that major structural decisions could be deferred and forces the council to find efficiencies from its own transformation initiatives rather than relying on LGR-driven savings it had anticipated.
findings.matters: Changes the planning horizon materially; forces identification of recurring savings that were supposed to come from reorganisation; affects the financial legacy left to successor authorities; increases the scale and urgency of local cost control.
findings.figures: At least one year delay to LGR; council now budgeting through 2028/29 instead of ceasing at 2028; 2028/29 deficit of £4.722m shifts to new authorities or EDDC depending on final timing
findings.quote: Although not confirmed it is now likely this will delay reorganisation by at least a year.

findings.matters: Any indication of planned council dissolution or restructuring is material to the council's finance director overseeing transition, to finance officers at peer councils monitoring how peers handle organisational change, and to lenders assessing the council's continued status and capacity to meet obligations.

findings.matters: One-off reserves mask the true scale of the structural problem in the current year; the real position emerges in future years when the council must have a strategy to address the gap

findings.detail: Central government grant funding is forecast to decline by £3.6m between 2026/27 and 2028/29. Transitional protection funding provides a buffer in 2027/28 but then rises in 2028/29, leaving the council exposed to the full scale of the grant cut by year three.
findings.matters: This is a material structural income loss that drives a significant portion of the forecast deficit and reflects sector-wide pressures

findings.headline: Council forecasts annual deficits of £3.86m (2027/28) and £4.72m (2028/29) with no identified funding plan
findings.detail: The MTFP shows budget requirements of £29.4m in both 2027/28 and 2028/29, but planned financing is only £24.7m each year, leaving structural deficits that must be covered by reserve drawdown, additional savings, or borrowing. The document does not indicate which of these will close the gap.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the scale of the shortfall, whether reserves are adequate to absorb multi-year deficits of this size, and what the council's strategy is for addressing it
findings.figures: 2027/28: budget requirement £29,404,248 vs financing £24,666,240 (deficit £3,861,338); 2028/29: requirement £29,404,248 vs financing £24,682,030 (deficit £4,722,217)

findings.headline: Interest income and minimum revenue provision assumptions are under review as possible budget items.
findings.detail: The strategy states interest income is held at £2m per year but is offset by "increasing borrowing and minimum revenue provision costs at £1.1m, however this cost is revisited below in the report as a possible saving item." This suggests the council may be considering changes to MRP policy to create savings, which could indicate rising debt levels.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's debt trajectory and whether it is using accounting policy changes to bridge budget gaps rather than sustainable savings.
findings.figures: Interest income £2m per year; MRP costs £1.1m; MRP is flagged as a "possible saving item."
findings.quote: Interest income is held at £2m per year, but this is offset by increasing borrowing and minimum revenue provision costs at £1.1m, however this cost is revisited below in the report as a possible saving item.

findings.headline: Council tax rise of 2.99% is built into the model but dependency on tax harmonisation in new authorities creates further uncertainty.
findings.detail: Council tax income is forecast at £12.068m in 2027/28 and £12.523m in 2028/29, assuming 2.99% rises. However, the strategy notes that 2028/29 income "is likely to be higher... through Council Tax harmonisation... this will a decision for the shadow authorities." East Devon's current council tax is "currently the lowest district tax in Devon," meaning harmonisation could be material but is not certain and will be decided by new authorities, not this council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know which income is within the council's control. Council tax harmonisation could improve the position or worsen it depending on the new authorities' choices.
findings.figures: Council tax forecast 2027/28 £12.068m, 2028/29 £12.523m, assuming 2.99% rises. East Devon has the lowest district tax in Devon.
findings.quote: income is forecast at £12.068m in 2027/28 and £12.523m in 2028/29... this is likely to be higher in 2028/29 through Council Tax harmonisation... East Devon's council tax is currently the lowest district tax in Devon.

findings.headline: Savings plans are uncertain and dependent on external legislative and contractual decisions outside the council's control.
findings.detail: The strategy identifies three main savings: planning fee reform (expecting £1.4m but prudently estimating £0.5m, with legislation timing uncertain and expected "end of calendar year"), leisure tender negotiation (at least £0.5m pending member debate and final contract terms), and capital programme review (modest £0.2m projected, review ongoing). None of these are committed or fully in the council's hands.
findings.matters: Uncertain savings create execution risk. A lender needs to know what savings the council can actually deliver, not what it hopes for.
findings.figures: Planning fee income: expected £1.4m, prudent estimate £0.5m. Leisure: at least £0.5m. Capital: £0.2m. Total identified mitigation ~£1.2m-£2.4m against deficits of £3.861m-£4.722m.
findings.quote: The long awaited planning fee income legislation bringing the cost of the service closer to break-even... is expected the end of the calendar year with increases to apply possibly in the last quarter of 2026/27. This should be in place for the 2027/28 budget. A broad estimated is this could achieve an additional £1.4m of income, but the exact details and timing is unknown, at a prudent level we could expect at least additional income of £0.5m in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Heavy reliance on drawing down reserves to balance budgets, with explicit acknowledgement of structural risk.
findings.detail: The council plans to use £2.7m-£3.9m from reserves to balance the 2027/28 budget, plus an additional £3m in reserve requests (LGR costs, internal resources, Marlcombe, EdenServ). The strategy explicitly identifies that "the key risk is that short-term balancing decisions in 2027/28 create a structural problem for 2028/29 and beyond." This is not a one-year smoothing but a multi-year reliance on drawing down reserves without a sustainable savings plan in place.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is unsustainable; a lender needs to know the council's true structural position and whether it can service debt once reserves are exhausted.
findings.figures: Available reserves £7.5m; call on reserves 2027/28 estimated £2.7m-£3.9m; additional reserve requests ~£3m; general fund balance reduced to £2.3m (12 months cover vs previous 18 months).
findings.quote: The key risk is that short-term balancing decisions in 2027/28 create a structural problem for 2028/29 and beyond.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficits driven by permanent loss of government funding.
findings.detail: The council faces £3.861m deficit in 2027/28 and £4.722m in 2028/29, driven by business rate rebasing and the ending of New Homes Bonus. These are not cyclical pressures but permanent reductions in the funding base. The strategy describes the financial position as having "fundamentally changed through external factors beyond the Council's control."
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's structural income can support its service commitments. Permanent funding loss is a risk to repayment ability.
findings.figures: 2027/28 budget requirement £28.528m vs funding £24.667m = £3.861m deficit. 2028/29 budget requirement £29.404m vs funding £24.682m = £4.722m deficit.
findings.quote: Changes made by Government in local authority funding allocations has significantly reduced monies available to EDDC in the time remaining before Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.detail: The Housing Ombudsman reports a 30% increase in determinations in 2024-25 and significant backlogs. Of East Devon's 43 escalated cases, 28 remain open with investigation targets set at 12 months. Closed cases have averaged 4.5 months to determination. findings.matters: Open ombudsman cases represent contingent liabilities whose final financial cost is unknown and could require reserve drawdown or budget re-prioritisation if maladministration is found

findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman determined 2 counts of severe maladministration in leasehold damp and mould cases, plus 10 maladministration and 6 service-failure findings
findings.detail: Of 43 cases escalated to the Housing Ombudsman in 2025/26, 15 have been determined. Two determinations found severe maladministration involving lack of action on damp and mould repairs in leasehold properties, where Section 20 processes contributed to delayed resolution. findings.paper_title: Annual complaint monitoring and service improvement report 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing complaints increased materially year-on-year (372 to 462 at stage 1; 135 to 182 at stage 2), with 80% upheld or partially upheld
findings.detail: Stage 1 housing complaints rose from 372 to 462, and stage 2 from 135 to 182. The council upheld or partially upheld 80% of stage 1 housing complaints, indicating substantive rather than frivolous failures. The main themes are property condition, repair delays and quality, and poor communication with tenants. The council appointed a Housing Performance Lead during the year to address complaint volumes and contracted root-cause work with weekly contractor meetings.
findings.matters: Escalating complaint volumes with high upheld rates indicate systematic service delivery problems in housing management that require remediation investment and suggest gaps in management oversight
findings.figures: Stage 1 complaints: 372 (2024/25) to 462 (2025/26); Stage 2: 135 to 182; 80% of Stage 1 Housing Complaints upheld/partially upheld
findings.quote: housing complaints have increased significantly over recent years. The main themes continue to relate to property condition, delays in completing repairs, the quality of repairs, and communication around appointmen ts.

findings.headline: Council is managing multiple significant capital and service projects (Recycling/Waste Contract, Leisure Services, Nutrient Award, New Town, CHP, Asset Management Plan) with significant service delivery implications
findings.detail: The Council has identified that it is involved in a number of key projects with significant implications for service delivery and residents, including a Recycling & Waste Contract, Leisure Services restructuring, a £4.2m Nutrient Award, CHP and New Town development, and a Business & Asset Management Plan for the Council House Stock. Governance has been enhanced through introduction of a Project Management Office.
findings.matters: Multiple concurrent major projects create execution risk and cash flow volatility; a lender needs to understand the timing, budget, and criticality of each to assess impact on council finances and whether there is sufficient capacity to manage them while maintaining core services.

findings.quote: Assurance Statements have identified the Council is currently involved in a number of key projects which have significant implications on service delivery and for the residents of East Devon: Recycling & Waste Contract, Leisure Services, £4.2m Nutrient Award, CHP & New Town, Business & Asset Management Plan for the Council House Stock.

findings.headline: Five of 16 mandated Local Government Transparency Code disclosures identified with compliance issues; 13 actions raised, 8 closed
findings.detail: Internal audit identified significant compliance issues for 5 of 16 mandated transparency code disclosures out of 13 actions raised. Eight actions have been closed; remaining actions are due October 2026. This indicates the council is currently not meeting statutory transparency requirements.
findings.matters: Transparency code breaches indicate weak controls over statutory compliance; a lender may question the robustness of the council's internal control environment if it is not meeting basic transparency and accountability requirements.
findings.figures: 5 of 16 mandated disclosures with significant compliance issues; 13 actions identified, 8 closed
findings.quote: SWAP found significant compliance issues for 5 of the 16 mandated disclosures.

findings.headline: Performance reporting identified as a current weakness in controls over Cabinet financial and performance management
findings.detail: Cabinet receives comprehensive budget monitoring reports on a frequent basis, but performance reporting has been highlighted as an improvement area and an acknowledged current weakness in controls. The council is rolling out a new key performance indicator system directorate by directorate, with supplier difficulties causing delays; full reporting is not expected until late in the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.matters: Without robust performance reporting to Cabinet, financial performance may not be identified or corrected promptly; this increases the risk of service underfunding or overspending being masked until it becomes a material issue.
findings.figures: Performance reporting delayed to late 2025/26 financial year
findings.quote: Although performance reporting has been highlighted as an improvement area and a current weakness in controls.

findings.headline: Several major strategic planning applications overturned on appeal or vulnerable to appeal, potentially impacting development strategy delivery
findings.detail: The Council has identified that several major strategic planning applications have been overturned on appeal or are vulnerable to appeal. This is described as impacting the ability to deliver the development strategy and return to healthy housing land supply. Procedures and processes are under review to make decision-making more robust.
findings.matters: Planning appeal losses on major applications indicate governance or technical weaknesses in a core council function; for lenders this signals risk to the council's capital strategy, development outcomes, and potentially to income-generating projects on council land.
findings.figures: Several major strategic applications; specific number and value not stated
findings.quote: Decision making of Planning Committee on major strategic applications with several decisions made and overturned on appeal or vulnerable to overturn on upcoming appeals. This could impact on our ability to deliver our development strategy and return to a healthy housing land supply

findings.headline: HRA reserves are below prudent levels and will take years to recover to sustainable levels
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has flagged that the Council's Housing Revenue Account requires planning to reinstate deemed minimum balances. The Council acknowledges a multi-year recovery period but reports that spending and income were controlled within budget for 2024/25 and 2025/26, evidencing emerging stability. A new Asset Management Plan and Business Plan will be presented in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender to a council with underfunded housing reserves faces higher risk; understanding the trajectory and timeline for reserve restoration is essential to lending decisions, particularly for borrowing against the HRA.
findings.figures: Multi-year recovery period required; 2 years of controlled budget outcomes in 2024/25 and 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council estimates that it will take a number of years to recover the HRA financial position which should include reserves and balances back at prudent levels and in year expenditure not exceeding income.

The council explicitly acknowledges this 'is going to require careful resourcing and prioritising.' findings.detail: The audit of supplier resilience—the council's ability to continue operating if a key supplier fails—received Limited assurance, meaning improvement is required. Five Priority 2 actions (medium-priority but material) were raised. This suggests the council has not adequately assessed or mitigated its exposure to supplier failure.
findings.matters: Supplier failure can disrupt council operations and service delivery. Weak resilience planning increases the risk that a single failure could cascade into service loss or financial loss for the council.

This represents deterioration from 2024/25 when 58% achieved Substantial or Reasonable assurance, suggesting the council's control environment is weakening rather than improving.
findings.matters: A widening gap in audit findings indicates the council's governance and controls are weakening, not strengthening, which increases financial and operational risk for anyone lending to or dealing with the council.

findings.headline: Contract Management identified as High Organisational Risk with no lead officer, no internal support, and four contracts not on the register
findings.detail: Internal audit identified systematic weaknesses in contract management: no named lead officer for strategic oversight, no internal resource for supporting contract managers or providing training, staff unaware of existing guidance, contracts lacking clear performance criteria, contract managers unable to demonstrate budget monitoring, inconsistent compliance with contract procedures, and four contracts not recorded on the council's contract register. The council has agreed 10 actions by end-September 2026.
findings.matters: Weak contract management directly enables service overspending, poor value for money, and creates vulnerability to fraud or corrupt practice. A lender needs confidence that the council can control and enforce its supplier contracts.
findings.figures: 10 agreed actions; September 2026 deadline; 4 contracts not recorded on council's register
findings.quote: There is no defined lead officer for strategic oversight of contract management, and no internal resource for supporting contract managers, providing training, or identifying and addressing poor practice.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register East Devon July 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Review poses risk of council dissolution and requires freeing up an estimated 25% organisational capacity.
findings.detail: The council faces significant uncertainty from potential devolution and Local Government Review, including potential redistribution of powers, resources, and council dissolution. To manage the transition smoothly, the council estimates it must free up approximately 25% capacity from existing projects and BAU activities. If this capacity cannot be released, there is high risk of missing LGR data return and service planning requirements.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty about the council's future, combined with major internal resource constraints, creates questions about continuity, strategic focus, and the council's ability to respond to new obligations.
findings.figures: Estimated 25% capacity requirement; transition to successor organisation.
findings.quote: If we are unable to free up capacity across the organisation (est 25% need) from existing projects, priorities and BAU, there is a high risk against meeting LGR data return and service planning requirements for a smooth transition to the succesor organisation.

This threatens to reduce productivity and the council's ability to meet statutory and other service responsibilities. A People Strategy was introduced with an implementation action plan, but the risk remains rated high.
findings.matters: Service delivery failure or compliance gaps from understaffing create operational risk; lenders care about whether the council can execute its statutory duties and strategic plans.

An updated MTFS will be presented in September 2026 to address this shortfall.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register East Devon July 2026
findings.headline: HRA overspent its entire earmarked reserves and now relies on borrowing to fund compliance expenditure.
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account spent exceptionally above budget in 2023/24, consuming all earmarked reserves. A revised 2024/25 budget required approval to cover compliance costs, which utilises part of the HRA Balance and increases borrowing. The council now needs to deliver savings from 2025/26 onwards to replenish reserves and afford this borrowing.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know about reserve depletion and reliance on new borrowing to fund operational costs—this signals reduced financial flexibility and increased debt service obligations.
findings.figures: All earmarked reserves utilised; increased borrowing required; savings required from 2025/26 onwards.
findings.quote: The Council expenditure in the HRA for the second half of 2023/24 was exceptionally high and significantly above the original budget which required utilising all earmarked reserves. A revised budget was required to be approved for 2024/25 to meet requirements of compliance expenditure which utilises part of the HRA Balance and increases borrowing. To afford the borrowing and replenish the Balance savings will be required to be delivered from 2025/26 onwards.

findings.headline: HRA under 'intense budget pressure' from policy-imposed income limits, economic headwinds, regulatory duties, and capital investment needs
findings.detail: The HRA faced sector-wide pressures including 'policy-imposed income limits, economic headwinds, new regulatory duties, and long-term capital investment needs'. The council's response included maximum rent rises, cost-cutting, use of reserves, and borrowing. The HRA balance restoration plan proceeds at £0.25m per annum, but the balance after this year's contribution is £2.5m against a target of £3.1m. The depreciation estimate was £0.2m lower than expected, requiring an additional revenue contribution to capital to manage borrowing costs.
findings.matters: The HRA is operating under policy constraints (capped rent increases) while facing economic and regulatory cost pressures. This is a sector-wide problem, but it means the council's housing business is under structural pressure. The balance restoration is slow and dependent on depreciation assumptions. For lenders, this signals ongoing tension in the HRA that may require borrowing or reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: Planned £0.25m transfer to HRA balance confirmed; surplus after contribution £2.5m; depreciation estimate £0.2m lower than expected; additional revenue contribution to capital being made
findings.quote: 2025/26 was a year of intense budget pressure for district council HRAs, shaped by policy-imposed income limits, economic headwinds, new regulatory duties, and long-term capital investment needs. Councils responded with a mix of maximum rent rises, cost-cutting, use of reserves, borrowing, and advocacy for policy change and central Government assistance.

findings.headline: Systemic staffing challenges across the council, with multiple services affected by vacant posts and recruitment difficulties
findings.detail: Recruitment and retention has been challenging across multiple service areas. Street Scene had vast majority of its £1.5m underspend driven by vacant posts 'throughout the year' with knock-on effects on transport costs. Climate Change Support Officer role remained unfilled all year (£0.2m saving). Public Health achieved £0.25m surplus 'due to staff turnover and recruiting issues'. Corporate Services had establishment-related variances. These vacancies directly reduced planned expenditure but also service capacity.
findings.matters: Persistent vacancy and turnover across multiple services suggests systemic staffing problems affecting service delivery and financial control. For a lender, this raises questions about management capacity to handle increased scrutiny during LGR preparation and ability to execute capital programmes and compliance requirements.
findings.figures: Street Scene: vast underspend 'the result of vacant posts throughout the year'; Climate Change: £0.2m from unfilled Support Officer role; Public Health: £0.25m from staff turnover and recruiting issues
findings.quote: The vast majority of the underspend in Street Scene is the result of vacant posts throughout the year as recruitment and retention has been challenging, particularly at the beginning of the financial year. This has also had the knock on effect of reduced Transport costs and spend within Supplies and Services due to the reduced capacity.

findings.headline: Capital programmes underspend by £38m with material slippage into 26/27, driven by team capacity constraints and procurement delays
findings.detail: Capital expenditure undershot budget by £38m (38% under budget). The largest underspends are: Regeneration Economy (£18m under), Beaches and Foreshores (£3.2m under), Public Conveniences (£4.5m under). The Property & Asset team took time to reach capacity through 25/26, with recruitment and onboarding of new managers prioritized over project delivery. Procurement lead times 'dictated by legislation' further delayed project starts. All underspends are being carried forward as slippage to 26/27.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage (especially in regeneration and strategic development) suggests execution risk and delivery capacity constraints. Deferring £38m of investment pushes cost and inflation pressure into 26/27 when the council is also facing LGR preparation costs. For lenders, this indicates the council may struggle to deliver planned capital programmes within timescale or budget.
findings.figures: Total capital underspend £38.0m against £48.6m budget; Regeneration Economy £18.0m under; Beaches and Foreshores £3.2m under; Public Conveniences £4.5m under
findings.quote: Although the capacity issues that drove the Capital underspend in 24/25 have now been addressed through recruitment, this has been phased throughout the year. The process of recruiting, onboarding and training of the new property and asset managers and officers has taken precedence in 25/26 in order to create a cohesive, driven team. These unavoidable delays have been exacerbated by the lengthy procurement lead times dictated by legislation, resulting in the start dates for a large number of the budgeted capital programmes and projects being rescheduled. The financial impact of this is predicted to be a significant underspend in year to be taken as slippage, to be delivered in 26/27.

findings.headline: HRA compliance spending significantly below budget due to recruitment and procurement delays, with emerging disrepair legal costs
findings.detail: Compliance-related HRA spend was significantly below budget following recruitment and procurement delays. The report acknowledges these issues are 'currently being addressed to enable much greater progress next financial year'. Additionally, disrepair legal costs were higher than anticipated and are described as 'notoriously difficult to predict'. The service has invested in new processes and expertise, but this suggests compliance work was deferred rather than completed.
findings.matters: Deferred compliance work in housing creates latent liability and regulatory risk. Disrepair legal costs being unpredictable and material signals a potential emerging obligation. For lenders, this indicates housing service capacity has been constrained and compliance backlog may create future cost spikes.
findings.figures: Compliance spend 'significantly below budget' (amount not quantified in commentary); disrepair legal costs higher than anticipated
findings.quote: Compliance related spend is significantly below budget following recruitment and procurement delays. These issues are currently being addressed to enable much greater progress next financial year and compliance KPIs remain on target. A small portion of this underspend has been offset by higher than anticipated expenditure on jobs that are excluded from the PPP within the IAMC contract and on higher then expected disrepair legal costs which are notoriously difficult to predict.

findings.headline: Car park income £0.4m below expectation, driven by tourism volatility and cost-of-living pressures
findings.detail: Car park income fell £0.4m short of budget due to reduced visitor volumes. The council attributes this to tourism-driven volatility (weather and water conditions), ongoing cost-of-living pressures reducing visitor numbers, and lifestyle changes such as hybrid working and lower high street footfall. The marginal increase versus 24/25 is described as 'in line with National statistical trends', suggesting the shortfall reflects structural changes rather than temporary setback.
findings.matters: For a small coastal district, car park income volatility signals both cyclical revenue risk and potential structural decline in visitor-dependent income. The causes identified (cost-of-living, hybrid working, lower footfall) suggest ongoing downside risk rather than a one-off issue.
findings.figures: £0.4m adverse variance on car park income; marginal increase versus 24/25
findings.quote: Car park income which was below expectations (£0.4m(A)) due to reduced volumes with parking permits partially offsetting what would have been a significant deficit. There are many factors impacting smaller districts such as EDDC across the country due to tourism‑driven volatility with weather & water conditions being significant factors. Ongoing cost‑of‑living pressures also reduce visitor numbers, plus other known lifestyle changes such as hybrid working and lower high street footfall.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing by £38.4m over three years to £187.5m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The underlying borrowing need (CFR) increases from £149.1m in 2025/26 to £187.5m in 2028/29, a growth of 26% in three years. This reflects substantial capital ambitions across both the General Fund and HRA.
findings.matters: Rapid CFR growth indicates either accelerating capital investment or extending debt repayment horizons. Lenders need to understand whether this reflects serviceability or capital intensity concerns.
findings.quote: Total CFR 123,093 149,139 160,546 179,040 187,506 (with rows for General Fund and HRA summing to these totals)

findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position, relying on reserves to defer borrowing while betting on interest rate falls
findings.detail: East Devon is deliberately not fully borrowing to fund its Capital Financing Requirement, instead using cash reserves as a temporary funding measure. This strategy assumes interest rates will fall significantly. The council explicitly states it will monitor rates and switch strategy 'if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a sharp FALL in borrowing rates, then borrowing will be postponed.'
findings.matters: This strategy creates refinancing risk and depends on interest rate forecasts proving correct. If rates rise unexpectedly or reserve balances fall, the council faces higher borrowing costs or constrained capital spending. The strategy also reveals confidence in rate forecasts that may not materialise.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing in 2026/27: £238k difference between CFR (£160,546k) and planned debt (£160,308k)
findings.quote: The Authority is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels... if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a sharp FALL in borrowing rates, then borrowing will be postponed.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme 2027/28 and 2028/29 subject to amendment pending Business Plan adoption
findings.detail: The document states that HRA capital expenditure estimates for future years are provisional: 'amounts may need to be amended and this Statement represented to Council once the Plan has been considered and adopted.' The document also flags potential impact from Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).
findings.matters: Uncertainty in the HRA capital programme creates forecasting risk for debt projections. Lenders need clarity on what capital spending is committed versus aspirational. LGR uncertainty is particularly material as it could trigger financial restructuring.
findings.figures: HRA capital 2027/28 £10,270k, 2028/29 £9,822k (marked as estimates subject to amendment)
findings.quote: The gross capital expenditure estimate for 2028/29 for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) capital programme has been added for 2027/28 and 2028/29 based on the working version of the HRA Business Plan, amounts may need to be amended and this Statement represented to Council once the Plan has been considered and adopted. Consideration may also be required in relation to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).

findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorating from 465% to 571% in four years
findings.detail: The ratio of HRA debt to annual revenues worsens from 464.83% in 2025/26 to 571.10% in 2028/29. This metric is a key leverage indicator showing the multiple of annual revenue that outstanding debt represents. The trend is upward throughout the forecast period.
findings.matters: A debt-to-revenue ratio above 500% signals high leverage and reduced debt service flexibility. Lenders use this metric to assess whether housing revenue streams can support debt repayment in stressed scenarios.
findings.quote: HRA ratio of debt to revenues... 464.83% (2025/26 Estimate) 504.52% (2026/27 Estimate) 538.79% (2027/28 Estimate) 571.10% (2028/29 Estimate)

findings.headline: LATCo mobilisation costs of £955k total (£641k + £314k) funded from capital receipts, not revenue
findings.detail: The council is establishing a Local Authority Trading Company for Recycling and Refuse, with mobilisation costs of £641k in 2025/26 and £314k in 2026/27 being funded through 'flexible use of capital receipts' from qualifying assets. This diverts capital receipts from capital projects to revenue-type costs.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts for revenue mobilisation costs reduces capital funding flexibility and potentially constrains the capital programme. The timing (alongside LGR uncertainty and the £60m housing programme) suggests capital resources are under pressure.
findings.quote: In the current year we are estimating costs associated with mobilisation of £641k and a further £314k in 2026/27. Funding of this qualifying expenditure will be by the application of the "flexible use of capital receipts" through receipt from qualifying assets i.e. the capital receipts available will be used to fund 2025/26 and 2026/27 expenditure.

findings.headline: Each £100k of capital spending creates £10k annual revenue cost obligation for 40 years
findings.detail: The document states that for every £100k of capital expenditure, the Medium Term Financial Plan bears an annual cost of approximately £10k for 40 years in MRP and interest. This means the £60m housing programme carries approximately £6m annual revenue cost for four decades.
findings.matters: This quantifies the true cost of capital spending and shows long-term revenue budget commitment. It should be cross-checked against the council's revenue budget sustainability and the MTFP.
findings.figures: £10k MTFP impact per £100k capital spend, over 40 years
findings.quote: It has been reported to members that broadly that for every £100k included, the impact of costs in the MTFP is £10k for 40 years.

findings.headline: HRA business plan and housing asset strategy not yet determined despite being critical to £60m housing programme
findings.detail: The capital strategy identifies the HRA business plan and housing asset strategy as 'an important factor yet to be determined' and defers consideration to 2026/27. This is the financial framework that must support the £60m housing borrowing, but it does not yet exist.
findings.matters: The strategy commits to borrowing £60m for housing without having completed the business plan that justifies and tests affordability of the debt. This is a material governance and planning gap.
findings.figures: Deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: An important factor yet to be determined is the HRA business plan and housing asset strategy with the associated capital programme and financing. This will be consider in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates planning uncertainty with successor authority due April 2028
findings.detail: The capital strategy acknowledges that a Local Government Reorganisation with a successor authority taking over from April 2028 must be considered. This is less than two years away and creates material uncertainty for multi-year capital programmes including the £60m housing commitment.
findings.matters: A fundamental restructuring of the council creates uncertainty for long-term capital delivery, debt servicing arrangements, and organisational continuity. Lenders need clarity on how this affects the viability of declared programmes.
findings.figures: April 2028
findings.quote: However, consideration has to be given to Local Government Reorganisation and the likely event of a successor authority being in place from April 2028.

findings.headline: £60 million prudential borrowing commitment for Build and Buy affordable housing programme
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow up to £60 million over five years to deliver 500 new homes through new-build delivery and strategic property acquisitions. Each scheme will be appraised against the Business Plan Financial Model, but the total commitment is already declared and expected to proceed.
findings.matters: A £60m borrowing commitment creates a 40-year revenue obligation and materially affects debt servicing. Lenders will need to understand the HRA's ability to carry this debt and the business case underpinning it.
findings.figures: up to £60 million of prudential borrowing to deliver 500 homes over the next five years
findings.quote: The Financing Strategy underpins the Council's Build and Buy Plan, enabling a programme of new-build delivery and strategic property acquisitions with up to £60 million of prudential borrowing to deliver 500 homes over the next five years.

findings.paper_title: Council 25 Feb 26 Council Tax Resolution 2026_27 new committee format template1
findings.headline: A £1m government funding gap in 2026/27 was closed only by a one-off adjustment grant; the structural shortfall returns from 2027/28 unless mitigated.
findings.detail: Government changed its business rates funding formula between Provisional Settlement (17 Dec 2025) and Final Settlement (9 Feb 2026), with just four days' notice. This created a £1m funding reduction for East Devon. MHCLG provided a one-off adjustment support grant of £1m to compensate for 2026/27 only. The council explicitly states this grant is a one-off payment, meaning the £1m reduction will hit 2027/28 onwards. This is a structural funding gap, not a timing issue, and the council acknowledges it will need to be addressed in the revised Medium Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that this council's 2026/27 budget depends on non-recurring government support and faces a material structural funding shortfall from 2027/28. This represents vulnerability to government policy changes and creates future budget pressure.
findings.figures: £1m reduction compared to Provisional Settlement; £1m one-off adjustment support grant for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: Currently this additional grant is stated as a one off payment for 2026/27 so this reduction in funding if not mitigated in future years will affect our budget estimates for 2027/28 onwards.

findings.headline: Working-age council tax arrears in receipt of support rose to 15.81% in December 2025, up 2.12 percentage points from December 2024
findings.detail: Working age CTR cases in arrears increased from 13.69% in December 2024 to 15.81% in December 2025. The paper attributes this to national increases in council tax arrears due to economic factors and notes that East Devon is experiencing a reduction in overall collection rates. Arrears vary significantly by support band: Band 1 (100% support) 13.66%, Band 2 (80% support) 16.59%, Band 4 (25% support) 17.57%.
findings.matters: Rising arrears among recipients of council tax reduction—the most vulnerable households—signal deteriorating economic conditions. For lenders, this indicates the council's revenue collection is under pressure even from subsidised taxpayers, affecting cash collection and potentially requiring reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: 15.81%, 13.69%, 2.12 percentage point rise, Band 1: 13.66%, Band 2: 16.59%, Band 4: 17.57%
findings.quote: Nationally council tax arrears are increasing due to economic factors, and East Devon is not immune to this as we are also experiencing a reduction in our overall collection rates.

findings.headline: Collection rate assumption has declined to 98.5% from 98.6%
findings.detail: East Devon has reduced its assumed council tax collection rate for 2026-27 to 98.5%, down from 98.6% in the previous year. The paper attributes this to 'estimated in year performance', indicating the council expects collection to be slightly weaker. This reduces the tax base by approximately 65 Band D equivalents compared to maintaining the prior rate, directly lowering forecast council tax income.
findings.matters: Collection rate assumptions are fundamental to budget forecasting; a decline suggests emerging collection pressures that could constrain available resources.
findings.figures: Collection rate 98.5% (previously 98.6%)
findings.quote: We have used a collection rate of 98.5% (previously 98.6%) to reflect estimated in year performance.

findings.headline: Internal audit recommendations are being implemented slowly, with only 40% actioned by year end despite 123 open items at Q3
findings.detail: At the end of Q3 2024/25, the council had 123 open internal audit recommendations outstanding. By year end, only 40% had been implemented. The auditor raised an improvement recommendation that management should be prompted to respond in a timely fashion. However, a subsequent report to Audit and Governance Committee in July 2025 showed 49 actions had been closed, indicating acceleration.
findings.matters: Slow implementation of audit recommendations indicates potential control weaknesses are not being remedied quickly; increases risk that identified issues escalate into significant problems during a period of financial stress.
findings.figures: 123 open recommendations at Q3 2024/25; 40% actioned by year end; 49 actions closed between end of year and July 2025
findings.quote: For 2024/25, there were 123 open recommendations to address by the end of Quarter 3... By year end, Internal Audit reported that 40% of their recommendations had been actioned.

findings.headline: Aging population structure will increase demand for council services, with 65+ population forecast to grow from 30% to 32.5% by 2027
findings.detail: East Devon has an older age profile (average age 51.3 years vs national average 40.4 years). The 65+ age range is forecast to grow from 30.1% of the population in 2017 to 32.5% by 2027 — more growth than any other age cohort. Total population is expected to increase by 13% (19,992 people) by 2031. An aging population significantly impacts service delivery and budgets for health, social care, housing and related services.
findings.matters: Demographic change creates persistent upward pressure on service costs and housing demand (particularly specialist/adapted stock), whilst tax base growth may lag. Combined with the council's current HRA financial weakness, this creates a challenging backdrop for service sustainability.
findings.figures: Current population 148,000; expected growth of 19,992 (13%) by 2031; average age 51.3 years (national 40.4); 65+ population forecast to grow from 30.1% (2017) to 32.5% (2027)
findings.quote: The population of East Devon has an older age profile with an average age of 51.3 years compared to the national average of 40.4 years. This trend is set to grow with the 65+ age range forecast to increase more than any other age range, growing from 30.1% of the population in 2017 to 32.5% by 2027.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme experienced significant slippage with £13 million shortfall against budget
findings.detail: At month 9, the General Fund capital budget of £35 million was forecast to deliver only £22 million (a 37% shortfall). Economy and Regeneration directorate had £4.7 million slippage due to difficulties identifying projects meeting required funding criteria; Street Scene had £8 million slippage. The 2025/26 capital programme is anticipated to recover to around £31 million.
findings.matters: Large capital slippages can indicate project management challenges, procurement delays, or difficulty identifying viable schemes; impacts on-time service delivery and asset maintenance; affects the council's ability to modernise and improve services.
findings.figures: Month 9 budget £35 million, forecast £22 million; Economy and Regeneration £4.7 million shortfall; Street Scene £8 million shortfall; 2025/26 anticipated £31 million
findings.quote: On the capital programme, month 9 data showed that there had been significant slippage in the planned General Fund capital spend (from a budget of £35 million to a forecast of £22 million). Affected areas included spend through the Economy and Regeneration directorate (£4.7 million) and through Street Scene (£8 million).

findings.headline: HRA borrowings increased significantly and General Fund had to inject £15.8 million in loans to prevent further external borrowing
findings.detail: HRA borrowings increased during 2024/25 after the July 2024 budget rebase. The council resorted to making total loans of £15.8 million from the General Fund to the HRA by year end to minimise the need for new external borrowing at a time of raised interest rates.
findings.matters: Increased debt service obligations reduce financial flexibility and indicate the HRA is not self-sustaining. Cross-subsidisation from the General Fund to the HRA weakens both and creates dependency; rising interest rates make this more costly.
findings.figures: General Fund loans to HRA totalled £15.8 million by 31 March 2025; HRA borrowings increased during 2024/25
findings.quote: We note that by the end of 2024/25, the General Fund had made total loans of some £15.8 million to the Housing Revenue Account to minimise the need for new external borrowing at a time of raised interest rates.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserves have fallen below the council's minimum prudent level and will take years to recover
findings.detail: HRA reserves stood at £1.764 million at 31 March 2025, below the assessed minimum prudent amount of £2.1 million (or £3.1 million with headroom). This deterioration was caused by unplanned overspends on repairs and maintenance in 2023/24 that had to be honoured in 2024/25, prompting a budget rebase in July 2024. The council estimates it will take multiple years to recover the HRA financial position and return reserves to prudent levels.
findings.matters: Low reserves significantly reduce the council's ability to manage unexpected costs or service pressures, particularly concerning given the aging population and rising service demands. It signals structural issues in HRA finances and increased financial fragility.
findings.figures: HRA reserve £1.764 million at 31 March 2025; minimum prudent amount £2.1 million (£3.1 million with headroom); recovery will take 'a number of years'
findings.quote: By the end of 2024/25, the balance stood at £1.764 million – and had therefore fallen below the Council's minimum prudent amount... The Council estimates that it will take a number of years to recover the HRA financial position which should include reserves and balances back at prudent levels and in year expenditure not exceeding income.

news_drafts.headline: East Devon forecasts £266k more investment income than budgeted, on holdings of about £51.1m
news_drafts.lead:
East Devon District Council expects to earn £266,000 more from investing its spare cash this year than it budgeted, according to the latest in-year check of spending against budget (budget monitoring). The month-four report went to the council's Cabinet on 16 September 2026. It lists the item as "Treasury investment receipts 266 (F)", the "F" marking a favourable variance.

The report puts the forecast down to the performance of funds the council runs in-house and funds managed by outside firms. These held about £51.1m in mid-August. The council had £11m in the government's Debt Management Account Deposit Facility, which takes deposits from public bodies, and £9m in money market funds, which pool short-term cash from many investors. A further £15.437m was in the Payden Sterling Reserve Fund and £15.666m in a fund run by Royal London Asset Management.

Managing the council's borrowing and investing of spare cash is known as treasury management. The report says the income forecast will be refined as the council completes its cash flow analysis, its work on when money is expected to come in and go out.
news_drafts.paper_title: Finance Report month 4 monitoring update Annual Treasury Management review 2025_26, 16/09/2026 Cabinet

news_drafts.headline: East Devon auditors need separate strategy to restore confidence in council accounts
news_drafts.lead: External auditors have told East Devon's Audit and Governance Committee they need a formal strategy to regain assurance over the council's financial statements. The committee will receive a separate regaining assurance strategy and capacity assessment alongside the external audit progress report. The development reflects wider strain on audit capacity: Grant Thornton's fee for auditing the council in 2025-26 has been set at £169,103, reflecting "increased work auditors must now undertake as well as the scarcity of audit firms willing to do this work." Planning delays occurred in July and August 2026 because of officer capacity to respond to audit queries, though auditors report being in a good position for the critical post-statement audit phase beginning in mid-September.
news_drafts.paper_title: External Audit Progress and Sector Update 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: East Devon faces permanent £3.8m budget deficit as government cuts funding
news_drafts.lead: East Devon Council faces permanent budget deficits of £3.861m in 2027/28 and £4.722m in 2028/29, driven by government decisions to cut funding allocations. These are not temporary pressures but permanent reductions in the money available to the council. The council plans to use reserves — money set aside — of between £2.7m and £3.9m to close the 2027/28 gap. However, the council's own financial strategy identifies that "the key risk is that short-term balancing decisions in 2027/28 create a structural problem for 2028/29 and beyond." The planned savings meant to prevent this remain limited. Planning fee reforms are expected to deliver £1.4m but are prudently assumed at £0.5m pending legislation due at year-end; a leisure contract renegotiation may deliver at least £0.5m.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annual complaint monitoring and service improvement report 2025-26
